news.2026-11-19-indonesie-hausse-taux-ro: Destry Damayanti, who heads the central bank according to Antara and Xinhua, presents the hike as a “pre-emptive” measure to stabilize the rupiah and keep inflation within target [2][4].
On November 17, the rupiah hit a record low of 18,285 to the dollar, according to Reuters [1]. After the announcement, it barely moved [1].

Pressure is also coming from Jakarta: Reuters cites the domestic political crisis, including the vice president's resignation and a wiretapping affair involving the police, and analysts are worried about public finances and the central bank's independence [1].
To attract foreign capital, BI is also relying on incentives for currency hedging: these transactions stood at about $14.1bn as of November 17 [2][5].
Key takeaway: Bank Indonesia is choosing to slow its economy to defend its currency. Raising rates makes rupiah investments pay more and should keep foreign capital in the country [2][5].

The central bank is swimming against the tide of a Fed preparing to raise its rates: the minutes of its October meeting, released the same day, show that almost all its officials consider further hikes likely [6]. The Antara agency sums it up: BI is raising rates “to defend itself against the Fed's decisions” [2].

The problem is also political. When investors doubt a central bank's independence or the government's budget discipline, a rate hike is not always enough: indeed, the rupiah barely reacted on Wednesday [1].

A weak rupiah makes everything the country pays for in dollars more expensive and increases companies' foreign-currency debt burdens. Higher rates, meanwhile, make loans more expensive for households and businesses: that is the price of defending the currency.

If you travel to Bali, your budget in euros goes further when the rupiah falls. But the signal matters more: when US rates rise, emerging countries often have to tighten at home, which can slow markets where many European companies sell.

How it works: why a central bank raises rates to defend its currency

A currency is a price: one set by supply and demand. When foreign investors pull their money out of Indonesia, they sell rupiah to buy dollars, and the rupiah falls. By raising its policy rate, the central bank increases the interest paid on rupiah investments, which gives investors a reason to keep them or buy more [2]. The price to pay: credit becomes more expensive for households and businesses, which slows the economy [5]. The bank can also help investors protect themselves against a future fall in the currency (currency hedging), so they are less hesitant to come in [2][5].

Target handily beats expectations thanks to $301 million in tariff refunds, a boost that won't be repeated

On Wednesday, November 18, US retail giant Target reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.65, versus about $2.07 expected. Nearly a fifth came from $301 million in tariff refunds, a one-off boost that the bank JPMorgan considers flattering [1][3].
In the third quarter of its fiscal year, reported on Wednesday, Target recorded $301 million in pre-tax tariff refunds, adding about $0.50 to its earnings per share [1].
With this contribution, adjusted earnings per share reached $2.65, well above the roughly $2.07 expected by analysts, a forecast that did not include these refunds [1].
Excluding the refunds, adjusted earnings per share came to $2.15, up about 21% year on year, according to Zacks [2]. Sales rose 7.1%, according to IBTimes [4].
Management raised its outlook for fiscal 2026. It includes about $2.14 per share in refunds already recorded since the start of the year, but no future refunds [1].
JPMorgan is keeping its “neutral” rating: in its view, the refunds “flattered” the quarter, and excluding refunds, earnings were roughly in line with its revised forecast [3].
Target thus heads into the holiday season, the most important for retailers, with a turnaround that is gaining speed, according to Benzinga [1].

Key takeaway: at Target, tariffs paid on imports are coming back onto the books as refunds, and this inflates reported earnings. These refunds account for nearly a fifth of the quarter's earnings per share ($0.50 out of $2.65) [1].

This is not the first time. In the previous quarter, Target recorded $994 million in refunds: $1.65 of its $4.11 earnings per share came from them [5]. For the fiscal year as a whole, the total already reaches about $2.14 per share [1].

For investors, the whole question is separating the one-off from the lasting. A refund does not repeat: what matters going forward is the sales and margins of the retail business itself. That is why JPMorgan looks at earnings excluding refunds, roughly in line with its expectations [3].
For the US economy, these figures also send a signal about consumption: sales up 7.1% at one of the country's major retailers, heading into the holidays, show households that keep spending [1][4].

You probably don't shop at Target, but its results serve as a thermometer for US consumer spending, which weighs heavily in the stock indices behind your savings. And when a company posts surprising earnings, always check whether they come from its business or from a one-off gain.

How it works: reported earnings, adjusted earnings and one-off gains

Earnings per share is the company's profit divided by its number of shares: it is the figure analysts compare with their forecasts. But some gains or losses happen only once, like a tax refund: they inflate a quarter's results without saying much about the health of the business. Analysts therefore strip them out to compare like with like [2][3]. At Target, it was $2.65 per share with the refunds and $2.15 without them [1][2]. A company that “beats expectations” thanks to a one-off gain is less convincing than one that beats them thanks to its sales [3].

news.2026-11-19-japon-exportations-recor: Japan: driven by chips, exports jump 20.5% to a record in October

Japan's Finance Ministry released October figures on Wednesday, November 18: exports rose 20.5% year on year to a record of about 11,770 billion yen, driven by chipmaking machines. Imports, inflated by oil, also hit a record [1][2].
Sales of semiconductor (microchip) equipment jumped 49.7% in value, and car sales 19.9% [1].
Exports to the United States rose 23.9%, and those to China 13.3% [1].
Imports rose 21.6% to about 12,250 billion yen, with imported oil 60.5% more expensive in value [1][2].
The trade deficit, at 476.5 billion yen, is the sixth in a row, but half the size of the roughly 956 billion expected [1][2].
Key takeaway: the global race for artificial intelligence is keeping Japan's chipmaking-machine factories busy, one of the country's strengths [1].
But in volume terms, exports rose only 5.8%: most of the increase comes from prices, not from more goods sold [1].
For you, it's a sign that AI-related demand remains strong. It benefits chipmaking-machine manufacturers, including European ones, but it rests partly on high prices [1].

news.2026-11-19-pays-bas-missiles-pont-c: Netherlands: Dutch missiles struck the Crimean Bridge, Moscow asks whether The Hague is “entering the war”

On Tuesday, November 17, Dutch company Destinus, based in Hengelo, said its missiles were the only foreign weapons used by Ukraine against the Crimean Bridge. On Wednesday the 18th, the Russian embassy in The Hague asked whether the Netherlands was “openly” joining the conflict [1][2][3].
According to Destinus, Ukraine fired 9 Ruta Block 1 cruise missiles, 7 of which hit the road section of the bridge [2][3].
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had praised the role of these missiles in the operation earlier on Tuesday [2].
On X, the Russian embassy wrote that Moscow “has been duly informed of Dutch involvement” and that “the admission has been duly noted” [1][2].
Dutch Defense Minister Dilan Yeşilgöz called these threats “unacceptable”: supplying equipment to Ukraine does not make the Netherlands a country at war, The Hague responded [1][2].

Key takeaway: in April, the Russian Defense Ministry published a list of European companies accused of helping Ukraine make weapons, including two Destinus sites in Hengelo; former President Dmitry Medvedev described them as possible targets [2][3].
The Crimean Bridge, opened by Vladimir Putin in 2018, is a key supply route to the peninsula occupied by Russia [2].
For you, it's a reminder that European arms factories working for Ukraine are in Moscow's sights. Russian pressure on supplier countries, including France, could step up a notch [2][3].

Spain: Thursday's rail strike is called off, but train drivers are keeping the November 23 strike

On Wednesday, November 18, the signal operators' union SCF called off the strike planned for Thursday the 19th at Adif, the Spanish rail network manager, after reaching an agreement. The train drivers' union Semaf is maintaining its walkout on Monday the 23rd at Renfe, eleven days before the snap general election [1][2][3][6].
According to SCF, Adif accepted “all the points” demanded, including signal operator staffing levels and limits on working time [2][3].
The Transport Ministry speaks of an “important commitment” with the CCOO, UGT and SCF unions, and says it wants to bring the others on board [2].
Semaf considers the ministry's proposals insufficient and is looking at new strike dates [2].
On Tuesday, the government also approved a 5.3% increase in the minimum wage for 2027, from 1,221 to 1,286 euros gross per month over 14 payments [4].
Key takeaway: rail workers are mainly demanding safety guarantees; UGT and CCOO say they have won progress on rail safety and working conditions [1][2].
The minimum wage increase, below the 7% demanded by unions but above the 4.9% recommended by experts, comes in the middle of the election campaign, which employers criticize [4][5].
For you, if you need to take the train in Spain on Monday, November 23, expect disruptions on Renfe lines. Check your journey before you leave [2][3].

news.2026-11-19-pologne-tusk-censure.tit: Poland: Donald Tusk survives a no-confidence motion launched by Morawiecki, amid a crisis over the Constitutional Tribunal
news.2026-11-19-pologne-tusk-censure.sum: The Sejm, Poland's lower house, rejected the no-confidence motion against Donald Tusk's government: only 200 deputies voted for it, when 231 were needed, and 242 voted against. The vote took place on Tuesday, November 17 [1][2].
news.2026-11-19-pologne-tusk-censure.poi: The motion came from the Development Plus group of former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki [1][2].
It was a “constructive” no-confidence motion: it proposed replacing Tusk with Marek Jurek, a longtime conservative figure [2].
All 442 deputies present voted, with no abstentions [2].
The government therefore remains in place until the general election scheduled for autumn 2027 [2].
news.2026-11-19-pologne-tusk-censure.why: Key takeaway: the vote comes in the middle of a battle over the Constitutional Tribunal, where the two camps are fighting over the legitimacy of the judges and control of the institution [2].
President Karol Nawrocki, who is close to the right, is blocking the appointments of judges sought by the government, and the European Commission has asked him to accept the new judges [3].
news.2026-11-19-pologne-tusk-censure.for: For you, the stability of Poland, a large EU country bordering Ukraine, matters for all of Europe. The government is holding on, but its standoff with the president will continue until the 2027 election [2][3].

news.2026-11-19-nigeria-police-etats.tit: Nigeria: with the Senate's green light, the reform creating state police forces now awaits only Tinubu's signature
news.2026-11-19-nigeria-police-etats.sum: On Wednesday, November 18, the Nigerian Senate ordered that the constitutional reform allowing the country's 36 states to create their own police forces be sent to President Bola Tinubu. All 36 state assemblies had approved it, an unprecedented result [1][2][3].
news.2026-11-19-nigeria-police-etats.poi: The text replaces the single national police force with two tiers: a federal police service and state police forces [4].
Approval from at least 24 of the 36 assemblies was required; the Clerk of the National Assembly, Kamoru Ogunlana, speaks of “100%” approval [4].
The Senate is also asking Tinubu to send a bill on the organization of the police, which is needed for the new forces to come into being [3].
Senator Ekong Samson acknowledged fears that governors could misuse these police forces for their own ends [3].
news.2026-11-19-nigeria-police-etats.why: Key takeaway: until now, all of Nigeria's police have been under the federal government in Abuja. The reform would give the governors of the 36 states their own forces, a revolution for this federal country [3][4].
After the signing, each state will still have to pass readiness tests and prove it can fund its police; otherwise, it will remain under the federal police [4].
news.2026-11-19-nigeria-police-etats.for: For you, the effect is indirect: nothing will change on the ground before Tinubu signs, followed by the laws and tests that must come next [3][4]. In the long run, security managed closer to the ground could reassure those who trade with the country.

news.2026-11-19-afrique-du-sud-ramaphosa: South Africa: in Silicon Valley, Ramaphosa wants to make his country an AI builder, not just a customer

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa is leading a delegation to California to attract investment in artificial intelligence (AI). On Tuesday, November 17, speaking at Stanford's business school, he acknowledged that “investment has been lacking” and called for partnerships [1][2][3].
Ramaphosa wants his country to design AI, not just use it [1].
According to him, South Africa already hosts nearly 70% of Africa's data centers, the buildings filled with computer servers [1].
A Microsoft report ranks the country 46th out of 147 economies for AI adoption [4].
He hopes for new commitments from US companies, on top of the roughly 600 already present in the country [2].
Key takeaway: Pretoria doesn't just want to rent out land for data centers, but to capture a larger share of the value created around them, such as skilled jobs [2][3].
The president ties this bet to employment: “we want AI to create jobs in South Africa,” he said during his visit [2].
For you, it's an example of emerging countries' race to attract AI investment. Europe, and France, are competing for the same data centers [1][3].

agenda.2026-12-09-france-senat-vote-budg: France: the Senate votes on the 2027 state budget

Unanimously rejected by the National Assembly on November 4 (458 votes against), the finance bill reaches the Senate in its original version: floor debate begins on November 20 and the vote on the bill as a whole is set for Wednesday, December 9 [1][2]. A joint committee will follow in mid-December, ahead of the constitutional deadline of December 17, after which the government could proceed by ordinance [1]: a key issue for the deficit and France's credit rating.
